method: I edited the tutor's base code to restructure the website layout and added new content. I chose to build an interactive flashlight teardown page. For writing, I organised sources by component—battery, filament, switch, casing—to argue that hidden layers connect code to materials.
related_work: This week I drew on Kate Crawford and Vladan Joler's Anatomy of an AI System (2018), which maps a device from mine to landfill, and iFixit's teardown guides for understanding internal components. I also used Sabbaghi and Behdad (2024) on discarded battery energy, and Verité's Commodity Atlas on tungsten supply chains. These sources help frame the flashlight's hidden layers: materials, labour, and afterlife.

results_discussion: Making: I modified the tutor's base website to match my aesthetic. I replaced the gradient background with a solid colour and widened the page layout for a cleaner look. On the home page, I added a favourite image as decoration. I also uploaded my mood board for this week, which collects visual references for the flashlight teardown. These choices make the site feel more personal and coherent, while still serving as a container for my research. The solid background reduces visual noise, and the wider layout gives more room for images and text. The mood board helps me organise my visual thinking alongside the written sources. The artefact is the updated website, with the mood board as a new addition.
title: W2
introduction: This week, we explored how information is transmitted through code and examined digital works for Project 0. Homework involves finding literature and references on flashlight teardowns. My question: how does code connect to physical objects? I will answer by writing a literature review and making an interactive flashlight teardown.
